summary: Updates RFC 3279 to specify algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 encoding for DSA and ECDSA signatures that use SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary:
A certificate says who signed it and with what algorithm. The algorithm is named by a number, an object identifier, that has to be registered before anyone can use it.

This document registers the identifiers needed for two kinds of digital signature, DSA and ECDSA, when the hash used inside them is one of the four newer SHA-2 hashes rather than SHA-1. It also fixes exactly how those identifiers are written into a certificate, so that two implementations read the same bytes the same way.

subtitle: Adds the SHA-2 hash functions, and the DSA and ECDSA signature algorithms that use them, to the Internet X.509 profile.

tldr.problem: The Internet X.509 certificate profile had identifiers for DSA and ECDSA signatures only with the older SHA-1 hash. When the SHA-2 family of hash functions became available, there was no agreed way to say in a certificate or revocation list that a DSA or ECDSA signature had been made with one of them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC names the four SHA-2 hash functions and their object identifiers, and then gives object identifiers for the six new signature algorithms: DSA with SHA-224 and SHA-256, and ECDSA with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. It fixes the encoding rules for each, in particular that the parameters field is omitted.
tldr.outcome: A certification authority can now sign with DSA or ECDSA using a SHA-2 hash and say so unambiguously in the certificate, and the identifiers themselves live in the ASN.1 modules of RFC 4055 and RFC 5480. The RFC updates RFC 3279; the weaker SHA-1 may still be used where a stated policy requires it.

today: RFC 5758 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 3279 to add DSA with SHA-224 and SHA-256, and ECDSA with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, to the Internet X.509 public key infrastructure profile.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
This specification defines the contents of the signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue and signature fields within Internet X.509 certificates and CRLs when these objects are signed using DSA or ECDSA with a SHA2 hash algorithm. Those fields are more fully described in RFC 5280. The document also identifies all four SHA2 hash algorithms for use in the Internet X.509 public key infrastructure.

The document profiles material presented in the Secure Hash Standard, in the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Standard and in the Digital Signature Standard. It updates Sections 2.1, 2.2.2 and 2.2.3 of RFC 3279. Note that RFC 5480 updates Sections 2.3.5, 3 and 5 of RFC 3279.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate carries two things that matter here: the algorithm identifier that says how it was signed, and the signature bytes themselves. This document fills in those details for the case where the signature algorithm is DSA or ECDSA and the hash is one of the SHA-2 family.

sections.title: The Four SHA-2 Hash Functions
sections.content:
This section identifies four additional hash algorithms for use with DSA and ECDSA in the Internet X.509 certificate and CRL profile. SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 produce a 224-bit, 256-bit, 384-bit and 512-bit hash of the input respectively, and are fully described in the Secure Hash Standard.

The hash functions are identified by object identifiers. The identifier for SHA-224 is joint-iso-itu-t(2) country(16) us(840) organization(1) gov(101) csor(3) nistalgorithm(4) hashalgs(2) 4, for SHA-256 the same arc with 1, for SHA-384 with 2, and for SHA-512 with 3.

When one of these object identifiers appears in an AlgorithmIdentifier, all implementations MUST accept both NULL and absent parameters as legal and equivalent encodings.

Conforming certification authority implementations SHOULD use SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 when generating certificates or CRLs, but MAY use SHA-1 if they have a stated policy that requires the use of this weaker algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The four hashes differ only in the size of the number they produce, and each has its own registered identifier. The rule about parameters matters in practice: a certificate may leave the parameters out or write an explicit NULL, and a reader has to accept both as the same thing.

sections.title: DSA with SHA-224 and SHA-256
sections.content:
DSA is defined in the Digital Signature Standard, was developed by the U.S. Government, and can be used in conjunction with a SHA2 hash function such as SHA-224 or SHA-256.

When SHA-224 is used the identifier is id-dsa-with-sha224, whose value is joint-iso-ccitt(2) country(16) us(840) organization(1) gov(101) csor(3) algorithms(4) id-dsa-with-sha2(3) 1. When SHA-256 is used the identifier is id-dsa-with-sha256, the same arc with 2.

When the id-dsa-with-sha224 or id-dsa-with-sha256 algorithm identifier appears in the algorithm field as an AlgorithmIdentifier, the encoding SHALL omit the parameters field. That is, the AlgorithmIdentifier SHALL be a SEQUENCE of one component, the OID id-dsa-with-sha224 or id-dsa-with-sha256. The encoding rules for DSA signature values are specified in RFC 3279.

Conforming certification authority implementations that generate DSA signatures for certificates or CRLs MUST generate such signatures in accordance with all the requirements in Sections 4.1, 4.5 and 4.6 of the Digital Signature Standard. They MAY generate such signatures in accordance with all the requirements and recommendations in that standard if they have a stated policy that requires conformance to it.
sections.plainLanguage: DSA gets two new identifiers, one for each of the two smaller SHA-2 hashes. Both are written into a certificate with no parameters at all, so the AlgorithmIdentifier holds just the identifier and nothing else.

sections.title: ECDSA with the SHA-2 Hash Functions
sections.content:
The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm is defined in the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Standard. The ASN.1 object identifiers used to specify that an ECDSA signature was generated using SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 are respectively ecdsa-with-SHA224, ecdsa-with-SHA256, ecdsa-with-SHA384 and ecdsa-with-SHA512, each with the value iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) ansi-X9-62(10045) signatures(4) ecdsa-with-SHA2(3) followed by 1, 2, 3 or 4.

When one of those identifiers appears in the algorithm field as an AlgorithmIdentifier, the encoding MUST omit the parameters field. The AlgorithmIdentifier SHALL be a SEQUENCE of one component, the OID ecdsa-with-SHA224, ecdsa-with-SHA256, ecdsa-with-SHA384 or ecdsa-with-SHA512.

Conforming certification authority implementations MUST specify the hash algorithm explicitly using these identifiers when encoding ECDSA signatures with SHA2 in certificates and CRLs. Conforming client implementations that process ECDSA signatures with any of the SHA2 hash algorithms when processing certificates and CRLs MUST recognize the corresponding identifiers. The encoding rules for ECDSA signature values are specified in RFC 3279 and in RFC 5480.

Conforming certification authority implementations that generate ECDSA signatures in certificates or CRLs MUST generate such signatures in accordance with all the requirements specified in Sections 7.2 and 7.3 of the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Standard, or with all the requirements specified in Section 4.1.3 of SEC 1. They MAY generate such signatures in accordance with all the requirements and recommendations in those documents if they have a stated policy that requires conformance to them.
sections.plainLanguage:
ECDSA gets four identifiers, one for each SHA-2 hash. As with DSA, the parameters field is left out entirely.

The rule about explicit hashes matters because ECDSA certificates that do not name a hash are ambiguous. A client that meets one of these identifiers must be able to recognise it.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content: The object identifiers of the SHA2 hash algorithms are in the ASN.1 module of RFC 4055, and the identifiers for DSA with SHA-224 and SHA-256 as well as ECDSA with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 are defined in the ASN.1 module of RFC 5480.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not carry its own module of definitions. The hash identifiers live in the RFC 4055 module and the signature identifiers in the RFC 5480 module, so a single ASN.1 file already describes them all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NIST has defined appropriate use of the hash functions in terms of the algorithm strengths and expected time frames for secure use in Special Publications 800-78-1, 800-57 and 800-107. These documents can be used as guides to choose appropriate key sizes for various security scenarios.

ANSI also provides security considerations for ECDSA in the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Standard, and those considerations may be used as a guide.
sections.plainLanguage: Choosing a hash and a key of the right size is a separate decision from choosing the identifier for them. The RFC points at the NIST and ANSI guidance for that, rather than repeating it.

data.title: Object identifiers
data.code:
id-dsa-with-sha224 OBJECT IDENTIFIER  ::=  { joint-iso-ccitt(2)
   country(16) us(840) organization(1) gov(101) csor(3)
   algorithms(4) id-dsa-with-sha2(3) 1 }.

id-dsa-with-sha256 OBJECT IDENTIFIER  ::=  { joint-iso-ccitt(2)
   country(16) us(840) organization(1) gov(101) csor(3)
   algorithms(4) id-dsa-with-sha2(3) 2 }.
